My older brother is on dialysis in another city in Germany and I've been managing his schedule and appointments remotely for two years while studying social work and working part-time. Lately I just feel numb when I call him. Like I'm going through the motions. That scares me.

The numbness you're describing makes sense, two years of holding someone's medical schedule from a distance while managing your own life is a lot, and emotional flatness is a common response to sustained stress, not a sign that you don't care. Can I ask: do you have anyone you talk to about what this is like for you, separate from the practical coordination? And when you say 'going through the motions,' is it the calls that feel hollow, or more of your life generally? If that numbness is spreading beyond the calls into other areas, that's worth raising with a counsellor or your GP. You're allowed to need support for yourself, not just logistics advice.

I'm a nursing student in Kenya and my cousin with a physical disability lives with me. My family abroad treats me like I should manage everything because I'm 'the medical one.' I've been doing this a year and I'm so tired. My imam says patience is a virtue, but honestly I'm losing mine.

Being 'the medical one' in the family is a role that can quietly absorb everything, and studying nursing doesn't mean you signed up to be someone's full-time carer. Your imam's words about patience are meaningful, and patience doesn't mean carrying it all alone. Two steps: have an honest conversation with your family abroad about what you actually do day to day, name specific tasks and hours so they understand the scale. Then ask for one concrete thing, whether that's financial help, a shared care schedule, or someone stepping in during your exam weeks. Your fatigue is real information, not a personal failing. Your nursing tutors may also know carer support options locally.

My cousin in another Spanish city was diagnosed with cancer a few months ago. I'm working part-time in biology and I've become her go-to person for researching treatment options. My Sikh community is supportive but I'm spending every evening reading medical papers I barely understand and I'm terrified of giving her wrong information.

It's clear you care deeply about your cousin, and carrying the fear of giving wrong information is a heavy weight. A quick filter: stick to information from her oncology team, national cancer organisations, and hospital resources, and run anything you find past her medical team before sharing it with her. That protects both of you. What would help more: narrowing your research time to one or two evenings a week rather than every night, or stepping back from the research role entirely and helping her prepare questions for her oncologist instead? You don't need to become her medical translator. You need to be her cousin. Her team is the right source for treatment decisions.

Let your family know plainly: 'I'm spending X hours per week on this. I need that time back for job-hunting.' If another family member could take on even one task, like picking up prescriptions or calling the pharmacy, that's a fair redistribution. Your career matters too, and you shouldn't have to choose between your uncle's care and your own future.

I handle her finances and call her daily, but she's starting to not recognise me on the phone. As an Indigenous person, losing that connection to her feels like losing part of my roots.

You don't have to replace yourself, but sharing the care with someone who understands the cultural dimension could help both of you. Her GP or a local Alzheimer's society can also advise on what stage-specific support is available.

My aunt has Parkinson's and I've been supporting her from Kenya for over five years. I work full-time in engineering. I'm not religious, so there's no faith community to lean on. A few colleagues know, but I keep it surface-level. Lately I'm just so drained.

Five years of distance caregiving while working full-time is a long stretch, and being drained makes complete sense. Without a faith community, your support network is smaller, but not nonexistent. Two things: first, consider going slightly deeper with one colleague. You don't have to share everything, just enough that someone at work knows what you're carrying. That alone can reduce the isolation. Second, Parkinson's organisations often have helplines or virtual caregiver groups that are free and don't require any faith affiliation. Being drained for this long isn't a character flaw. It's a signal that you need something sustainable, not just willpower.

My boyfriend has long COVID and we're apart while I do my biology apprenticeship in the Netherlands. Six months in and I call him every day but some days he can barely talk from the fatigue. I feel like I'm watching him disappear and there's nothing I can do from here.

Watching someone you love fade into fatigue and feeling powerless across a distance. That's genuinely painful, and the daily calls show real commitment even when they're silent ones. Let me ask: when he's too tired to talk, have you tried just being on the line without expectation, or sending voice notes he can listen to when he has energy? Sometimes presence matters more than conversation. And do you have someone you talk to about this, a friend, your church community, or a counsellor at your apprenticeship programme? You're carrying grief alongside the caring, and that shouldn't sit alone.

My girlfriend has a genetic illness and lives far from me here in Mexico. I'm 18, working full-time, and I've been trying to support her for about a year. Lately the distance feels heavier and I wonder if I'm enough for her. Some nights I just feel completely hollow.

Feeling hollow at 18 while carrying a year of long-distance caregiving on top of full-time work. That's a lot, and I want to gently check on what 'hollow' means for you right now. Are you having any thoughts that you might not be okay, or that you'd rather not be here? If so, please tell someone today, a GP, a crisis line, anyone who can sit with you properly. That matters more than any caregiving advice. Beyond that: do you have anyone in your life, a friend, family member, or a Hindu community connection, who you could be honest with about how heavy this has gotten? You shouldn't be the only one holding this.

My older sibling has early-onset Alzheimer's and lives with me here in Ireland. Six months in and I'm doing engineering part-time while managing everything. Some days I walk in and they don't recognise me properly and I just fall apart. I don't know how to study and do this.

Being unrecognised by your own sibling. There's no preparation for that kind of moment, and falling apart is a completely human response, not a sign you're failing. Balancing engineering studies with co-resident dementia care is genuinely one of the hardest juggling acts. Two things: ask your university's disability or wellbeing service about carer adjustments, many allow flexible deadlines or reduced loads. And reach out to the Alzheimer Society of Ireland, who understand young carers specifically and can offer both practical strategies and someone to talk to. You don't have to hold this with just your own two hands.

I recently graduated in social work and I'm job-seeking in the UK. I live with my uncle who has depression. It's been this way as long as I can remember. I know the theory, I studied it, but I can't find anything online that helps me separate being a carer from being a social work graduate. Everything blurs together.

That's a uniquely frustrating position. You have the professional knowledge but the personal experience of living with your uncle's depression for years means you can't just switch to 'social worker mode' at home. The resources don't address that overlap because they're written for one role or the other, never both. Two things: your university's wellbeing service or a carer organisation might offer support specifically for people in caring professions who are also family carers, and supervision or peer support with other social workers who have personal caregiving experience could help you untangle the roles. You deserve support that sees both, not just one.

I study and work part-time in law here in Vietnam. My mum has schizophrenia and I live with her. It's been a few months since her diagnosis. Everything online is either in English or terrifying. I just want straightforward, practical information in Vietnamese that won't give me nightmares.

A new schizophrenia diagnosis for your mum, in a language you can't easily find good resources in, while everything you do find is either inaccessible or frightening. That's a terrible combination when you're already adjusting. Two practical steps: ask your mum's psychiatrist or the local mental health centre for Vietnamese-language family resources. They often have printed guides or can recommend local organisations that produce clear, non-alarmist content, and national mental health associations in Vietnam may have family sections written in plain Vietnamese. Avoid forums and unverified pages, stick to sources linked to hospitals or recognised organisations. What's the question you most need answered first, medication, daily support, or understanding what to expect?

I'm a history student in Mexico and my girlfriend has dementia, we've lived together for over five years. I'm Hindu and everything online about dementia caregiving for partners our age doesn't exist, let alone anything that speaks to my faith. I feel like I'm making it up as I go.

Over five years caring for a partner with dementia at your age, while trying to hold onto a faith lens that no resource seems to acknowledge, the fact that you feel like you're making it up as you go makes complete sense, because in many ways you are. The resources for young partner-carers of people with dementia are almost nonexistent. Let me ask: what's feeling hardest to navigate right now, the practical day-to-day of supporting your girlfriend, the emotional weight of watching someone you love change, or the spiritual question of how to make sense of this through your Hindu practice? Each of those might lead somewhere different, and your temple community could be a powerful source of support for the spiritual layer.

For the partner-specific emotional support, a general young-carer organisation may understand your situation better than a TBI-specific one. You deserve support that fits where you actually are.

A named, bounded task is easier to accept than 'help more.' And if the clinic sends appointment confirmations, see if those can auto-populate or be forwarded directly. You built the scaffolding. Now the goal is slowly pulling others onto it.

Try sitting down together and asking which tasks she'd prefer to own, even small ones. The goal isn't equal load, her condition may mean that's not realistic, but a task she chose is different from one she was assigned. Even one or two items she holds can shift the dynamic.

The phone alarm was a good start. The next layer is something that confirms rather than just reminds.

My mum is in Toronto being treated for cancer and I'm a graphic design apprentice here in Vancouver. Two years of long-distance supporting her, calling her oncologist, managing her appointments, talking her through chemo nights. My Jewish faith values caring for family but I'm drowning in my apprenticeship and I feel like I'm failing everyone.

Two years of supporting your mum through cancer treatment from across the country. That's an extraordinary amount of sustained care, and feeling like you're failing doesn't make it true. Your Jewish value of caring for family is clearly lived, not just believed. Two practical things: first, ask your mum's oncology team whether they have a social worker or cancer care coordinator who can handle appointment scheduling and be your on-the-ground contact. Most cancer centres do, and it can significantly reduce what falls to you. Second, please contact a cancer support organisation like the Canadian Cancer Society. They offer helplines, peer support, and resources specifically for family carers, including distance carers. You're not failing. You're overstretched, and those are different things.

My dad's on dialysis and I moved back home to Brazil a few months ago to help. I work part-time in biology and try to manage his diet, appointments, and meds. My Hindu faith says duty to parents is sacred, but I haven't seen my friends or had a proper conversation with my partner in weeks. Everything is about his schedule.

Dialysis care is relentless, and when every day orbits his schedule, your own relationships quietly fade. That's a real loss, not a minor one. Honouring duty doesn't have to mean disappearing as a person. Two things to help me guide you: does your dad's renal team have a dietitian or social worker who could take some of the diet and appointment coordination off your plate? And could you pick one fixed evening a week, even just two hours, where a friend or neighbour sits with him so you see your partner or friends?

I've been supporting my grandmother's diabetes care from Spain for as long as I can remember. I'm studying economics and working part-time, and I coordinate her meds and appointments with her local clinic by phone. But my own thesis is due and I've written almost nothing in three weeks. I can't split my brain anymore.

Splitting your brain between thesis writing and coordinating your grandmother's care from another country for years is genuinely unsustainable, and three weeks of almost no output is the evidence. Try a time-boxed approach: set a strict daily window, even 90 minutes, where you put your phone on silent and work only on the thesis, then return calls after. Tell her clinic your available call-back hours so they stop reaching you at random times. Your university's student support service may also grant extensions for carers, one email to ask costs nothing.

Also ask your granddad's MS nurse or local social services about a morning care visit, even one paid carer for an hour could free you to get to class. Your faith gives you strength, but practical support is what will change your daily reality.

My uncle's early-onset Alzheimer's has been about a year. I'm in Madrid looking for engineering work and he's in Manila. He calls me at odd hours convinced I'm someone else, and when I correct him he gets upset. My family says just to go along with it but that feels dishonest.

That tension between honesty and your family's instinct to go along with it is one of the most common and difficult dilemmas in Alzheimer's care, and there's no single right answer. A question that might help us think it through: when you correct him, is the upset worse than if you'd just let the mistaken identity sit for that call? Some families find that gentle redirection, not lying, but not correcting either, works better than either extreme. Something like 'I'm your niece and I'm here to talk' said warmly rather than 'no, I'm not who you think.' And does the odd-hour calling happen often enough that it's affecting your sleep and job search? If so, his care team may have ideas about managing sundowning and sleep patterns.

That gives you a boundary so you're not just waiting in the dark. Second, do they have someone physically nearby who could do a welfare check? And honestly, the impact this is having on your own wellbeing matters too. Have you talked to your GP about what you're carrying?

You know the clinical stakes, which makes her dismissal even harder to sit with, but 'stop nagging' suggests she may be experiencing your concern as pressure rather than support, even though it comes from love. Sometimes the most useful thing is to step back from the health conversation entirely and just be her cousin, send something funny, talk about something other than CF. You could also ask if she'd let you come to one clinic appointment with her, if distance allows, being alongside is different from checking up.

My girlfriend was diagnosed with schizophrenia a few months ago. I'm studying engineering part-time in Adelaide, she's in Perth. Sometimes she texts me convinced someone is watching her and gets angry when I say I don't see it. I feel terrible for not believing her.

It's genuinely confusing territory, wanting to be supportive while not reinforcing something you can't see, and feeling like either response is wrong. A question worth exploring: when she texts about being watched, is she asking you to agree, or is she looking for you to stay calm and present with her? Sometimes the most helpful response isn't agreeing or disagreeing but saying something like 'that sounds really frightening. I'm here with you.' You don't have to share her reality to stay connected to her distress. And has she got a care team you could contact about these episodes? Early schizophrenia support often includes family education, and knowing her triggers and warning signs would help you respond in a way that feels right to both of you.

My uncle has epilepsy and lives with me here in Stockholm. I've cared for him my whole life. He's started refusing to take his medication on days he 'feels fine,' says he doesn't need it. I've tried explaining the risks but he says I'm treating him like a child.

That's a familiar friction. He's an adult making a choice about his own body, and you're the one who sees the consequences if it goes wrong. A couple of things to consider: would he respond differently if the explanation came from his neurologist rather than from you? Sometimes the same information lands differently from a clinician because it doesn't carry the family dynamic. And is there a middle ground, for instance, a medication review where the doctor explains why the 'feeling fine' days are actually the proof the medication is working, not a reason to stop? If he has an epilepsy nurse, they're often skilled at having exactly this conversation. You shouldn't have to be the one making the case every time.

You're right not to dismiss it. Please don't carry this alone: ask her directly and gently, 'when you say things like that, are you saying you're tired of the illness, or are you saying you don't want to be here?' That question doesn't put ideas in someone's head. It opens a door. And if you're worried, please contact Lifeline on 13 11 14 or encourage her to reach out to her GP or a crisis line in Brisbane. Your nursing training doesn't mean you should assess this by yourself, she needs professional support, and so do you.

You can't be the safety net from a different island, and you shouldn't have to be. His care team can help build that plan.

Two years of notebook-and-reminders is real dedication, and it makes sense that job interviews throw a wrench in. They demand your full attention at exactly the moment care routines need to keep running. A couple of practical fixes: move supplement reminders into a shared app like Medisafe so your friend can see and acknowledge them themselves, and identify one backup person, another friend, a neighbour, who can cover an hour or two when you have interviews. You're job-hunting and caregiving simultaneously. Having a fallback for both isn't optional anymore, it's how you keep going.

That might close the distance gap more than another chat would. If being out of the loop is also feeding worry, talking to your sibling about a brief daily check-in, even just a one-line text, might help too.
